13140:
To regurgitate something means to bring it back up or push it back out — in other words, something that went in is now coming back out, usually without much change to it.

This word has two layers of meaning: one is physical and literal, and the other is mental and figurative. Both share the same core idea.

To regurgitate means to bring food or liquid back up from the stomach and out through the mouth.

It's similar to vomiting, but not quite the same. Vomiting is usually forceful and involves digested or partially digested food. Regurgitation is typically more passive and effortless, and the food or liquid often comes up in a form that is relatively unchanged — as if it barely got processed.

Examples:

  • A baby often regurgitates a little milk after feeding. This is sometimes called "spitting up."
  • A bird regurgitates chewed-up food into its chick's mouth to feed it.
  • A cow regurgitates grass from its stomach back into its mouth to chew it again. (This is called "chewing the cud.")

So in the physical sense, the word describes the backward movement of something from inside the body back to the outside, usually through the mouth.

This is the meaning you'll encounter far more often in everyday conversation and writing.

To regurgitate information means to repeat or reproduce something you've heard, read, or memorized — word for word or almost exactly — without truly understanding, processing, or thinking about it.

Just like food that gets regurgitated hasn't been properly digested by the body, regurgitated information hasn't been properly "digested" by the mind. You're just pushing it back out the way it came in.

Examples:

  • A student who regurgitates facts on an exam is someone who simply memorized the textbook and wrote it all down — without actually understanding what any of it means.
  • A speaker who just regurgitates whatever they read online, without checking if it's true or thinking critically about it, is not adding any value.
  • If someone asks you what you think about a topic and you regurgitate your teacher's opinion word for word instead of forming your own view, you are regurgitating.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This word almost always carries a negative or critical tone when used in the figurative sense. When you call something "regurgitated," you're suggesting it is:

  • Unoriginal — it's a copy, not a creation.
  • Mindless — no real thought went into it.
  • Lazy — the person didn't engage deeply with the material.
  • Hollow — it sounds like the real thing, but it's empty inside.

For example, saying "That essay just regurgitates other people's ideas" is a criticism. It means the writer didn't bring any independent thinking — they just replayed what others said.
The Key Difference: Regurgitating vs. Understanding

This contrast is important to understand the word fully:

  • When you understand something, you absorb it, connect it to what you already know, make sense of it in your own way, and can explain it in your own words. You've truly "digested" it.
  • When you regurgitate something, you take it in and spit it back out exactly as it was — unchanged, unexamined, unprocessed.

A parrot that mimics your words doesn't understand language — it just regurgitates sounds. That's a perfect image for what this word means intellectually.

Here are a variety of sentences to show you the full range of this word in action:

  • "Don't just regurgitate the definition — explain what it means in your own words."
  • "The politician's speech was boring because he simply regurgitated the same talking points he always uses."
  • "The report regurgitated statistics from a decade ago without offering any fresh analysis."
  • "Social media tends to regurgitate the same viral stories over and over again."
  • "The baby regurgitated some milk after feeding." (literal)
  • "A good education teaches you to think critically, not just to regurgitate information."
Words That Are Similar in Meaning (Figurative Sense)

To help cement your understanding, here are words that share the same idea:

  • Parrot (verb) — to repeat exactly what someone else said, without understanding.
  • Recite — to repeat memorized words aloud (though this word is more neutral; it doesn't always imply a lack of understanding).
  • Rehash — to present old ideas again, just slightly rearranged.
  • Reproduce — to copy and put out again.
  • Regurgitate is stronger and more negative than all of the above — it carries that slightly unpleasant physical image on purpose, to suggest that what's coming out is raw, unprocessed, and a little distasteful.

Regurgitate means: what went in came right back out, untouched by thought, process, or transformation. Whether it's food leaving a stomach or facts leaving a mouth, the idea is the same — no real digestion happened. The word is used most powerfully as a criticism of intellectual laziness, of people who repeat without reflecting, copy without creating, or speak without understanding.
13141: Regurgitation means the act of something flowing backwards — moving in the opposite direction from the way it is supposed to go. Think of it as a "reverse journey." Whether it's food, liquid, or even information, regurgitation describes something coming back the wrong way, often back to where it started.
The Most Common Meaning: Food Coming Back Up

The most familiar use of regurgitation is about food or liquid that has been swallowed coming back up through the throat and into the mouth.

Here's the key idea: your digestive system is designed as a one-way road — food goes in your mouth, travels down your throat, enters your stomach, and moves onward through your body. Regurgitation is when that food or liquid reverses course and travels back upward.

How is it different from vomiting?

This is an important distinction that many people miss.

Vomiting is a violent, forceful act. Your body actively uses strong stomach muscle contractions to push contents up. It is usually preceded by nausea, and the experience is unpleasant and dramatic. Your body is working hard to expel something.

Regurgitation, by contrast, is effortless and passive. There is no heaving, no nausea, no buildup. The food or liquid simply drifts back up on its own, like water flowing backwards through a pipe. A person might not even feel it coming — it just arrives back in the mouth quietly.

A common everyday example is acid reflux, where stomach acid and partially digested food gently rise back into the throat or mouth. That burning feeling in your chest or the sour taste you suddenly notice in your mouth? That's regurgitation.

Another example: babies frequently regurgitate milk after feeding — a small amount simply flows back up. This is sometimes called "spitting up," and it is completely normal in infants because the muscle that keeps the stomach sealed (called the lower esophageal sphincter) is not yet fully mature.
In Medicine: Regurgitation of the Heart

Doctors use the word regurgitation in a very important medical context: heart valve regurgitation.

Your heart has four valves that work like one-way doors. Blood flows through each valve in one direction, and then the valve snaps shut to stop any blood from flowing backwards. This is how your heart pumps blood efficiently throughout your body.

When a valve is damaged or doesn't close properly, blood leaks backwards through it. This reverse leaking is called regurgitation.

For example:

  • Mitral regurgitation means blood is leaking backwards through the mitral valve.
  • Aortic regurgitation means blood is flowing back through the aortic valve in the wrong direction.

In all these cases, the same core idea applies: something is going the wrong way — backwards, when it should be moving forwards.
In Nature: How Some Animals Feed Their Young

Regurgitation is also used to describe a feeding behavior seen in many birds and some other animals.

A mother bird, for instance, will eat food, begin to digest it in her own stomach, and then bring it back up — regurgitate it — into the mouths of her chicks who are waiting in the nest. The partially digested food is actually easier for the young ones to process. Pelicans, pigeons, penguins, and many other birds do this naturally.

This is one of the few contexts where regurgitation is seen as a positive, nurturing act. The word here simply describes food making a deliberate journey: down into the parent, and then back up and out to feed the offspring.

There is a very widely used figurative meaning of regurgitation, especially in education and intellectual discussion.

When someone regurgitates information, it means they are repeating something they have heard or read exactly as they received it, without truly understanding it, thinking about it, or processing it in any meaningful way.

Imagine a student who spends the night before an exam memorizing a list of historical dates. In the exam, they write those dates back down — word for word — without having the slightest idea of why those events were significant or how they connect to each other. They are simply spitting back out what went in. That is intellectual regurgitation.

The word carries a slightly negative or critical tone when used this way. It implies shallowness — an absence of genuine understanding. Someone who truly learns something transforms it in their mind; someone who merely regurgitates it is like a machine that stores and replays, rather than a mind that thinks and understands.

You might hear sentences like:

  • "His essay was just a regurgitation of the textbook."
  • "I don't want regurgitation of facts — I want you to think critically."

No matter the context — food, blood, animal feeding, or ideas — the word regurgitation always carries this single, unifying idea:

Something moving backwards, returning to a place it already passed through, or being expelled back the way it originally came in.

ContextWhat is flowing backwards or being repeated without processing?

In the body, it's food or liquid reversing up from the stomach. In the heart, it's blood leaking the wrong way through a valve. In nature, it's a parent returning food to feed young ones. In learning, it's ideas being repeated without understanding.

The common thread is always the same: a reversal, a backward flow, a return without transformation.
13142:
To rehabilitate something or someone means to restore them to a good condition after they have been damaged, broken, or fallen from an acceptable state.

Think of it this way: something was once good → then it got bad, broken, or lost → you work to bring it back to good. That process of bringing it back is rehabilitating it.

The word almost always carries the sense of effort and process — it's not an instant fix, but a deliberate, often gradual restoration.
The Four Main Ways It's Used

1. Rehabilitating a Person's Health (Medical)

This is the most common use you'll encounter. When someone suffers an injury, illness, stroke, surgery, or addiction, they often need help regaining their physical or mental abilities. The process of helping them recover and function again is rehabilitation.

"After his knee surgery, the doctors rehabilitated him over several months until he could walk normally again."

"The clinic rehabilitates patients recovering from addiction."

A key point: it's not just treating the immediate problem. It's the longer journey of rebuilding the person's ability to live, move, or function as they did before — or as well as possible.

2. Rehabilitating a Criminal or Offender (Social)

This use is about people who have broken laws or social norms. To rehabilitate them means to guide and help them change their behavior, develop skills, and become a responsible, productive member of society again.

"The goal of the prison program is not just punishment — it is to rehabilitate offenders so they don't commit crimes again."

This is different from simply punishing someone. Punishment says you did wrong and must suffer a consequence. Rehabilitation says we want to change you so you can do right in the future.

3. Rehabilitating a Reputation (Social/Professional)

A person's reputation, name, or public image can be damaged — by a scandal, a false accusation, a mistake, or unfair judgment. To rehabilitate their reputation means to restore their good standing in the eyes of others.

"After the investigation proved he was innocent, years of work were done to rehabilitate his reputation."

"The politician tried to rehabilitate her image after the controversy."

Notice here the object is not the physical person but their reputation — their standing in society.

4. Rehabilitating a Building, Place, or Land (Physical Restoration)

Objects and places can be rehabilitated too. An old, crumbling building, a polluted river, or a neglected neighborhood can all be rehabilitated — meaning restored to a functional, healthy, or valuable state.

"The city spent millions rehabilitating the historic old theatre."

"Environmental scientists are working to rehabilitate the wetlands destroyed by pollution."
The Less Common But Important Use: Rehabilitating an Idea or Concept

Sometimes an idea, theory, or way of thinking falls out of favor — people stop taking it seriously or it gets discredited. When scholars or thinkers bring it back to respectability and treat it as worth considering again, they are said to rehabilitate it.

"Some modern philosophers have tried to rehabilitate the moral theories that were dismissed in the 20th century."
The One Thread That Connects All Uses

No matter the context, these three elements are almost always present when you use rehabilitate:

  • Something was once in a better state.
  • It deteriorated, was damaged, or fell from that state.
  • Deliberate effort is being made to restore it.

If any of these three elements is missing, rehabilitate is probably not the right word.

• It is not the same as simply fixing or repairing something minor. You wouldn't say "I rehabilitated my broken pen." The word implies a more significant, meaningful, or systemic restoration.
  • It is not the same as punishing someone. In fact, in criminal justice, rehabilitation and punishment are often presented as opposing philosophies.
  • It is not creating something new. You're always restoring something that previously existed in a better form.

When you use this verb, here is what typically plays each role:

Who/what does the rehabilitating?
Doctors, therapists, governments, programs, organizations, communities, time, evidence — entities with the power and intent to restore something.

Who/what gets rehabilitated?
A patient, a criminal, a building, a reputation, an ecosystem, an idea — anything that was once in a better state and needs to be brought back.

Rehabilitate carries a tone of compassion, effort, and hope. It assumes that whatever is damaged is worth restoring and capable of being restored. When a society debates whether to rehabilitate criminals rather than simply imprison them, it is having a deep moral debate about whether people can change and whether they deserve that chance. The word is never neutral — it implies a belief in the possibility of recovery.

Whenever you're unsure if rehabilitate is the right word, ask yourself:

"Was this once better? Did it fall from that? Is someone working to bring it back?"

If the answer to all three is yes — rehabilitate fits perfectly.
13143:
To rehash something means to take old material — old ideas, old arguments, old information — and present it again, but in a slightly different form, without adding anything genuinely new or valuable.

The key here is that combination: old content + superficial reworking + nothing of real substance added.
A simple image to lock it in

Think of last night's leftovers. Someone takes them, chops them up a bit, rearranges them on a new plate, and serves them as today's meal. It looks slightly different from yesterday. But it's fundamentally the same food. Nothing new was created.

That is exactly what it means to rehash something. The "dish" — the idea, the argument, the content — is old. The slight reworking is just cosmetic. No real value has been added.

Rehash is almost always a criticism. When you say someone rehashed something, you are implying they were lazy, unoriginal, or uninspired. You are saying: "This person didn't bring anything new to the table. They just dressed up old ideas in slightly new clothes."

This makes it different from neutral words like review or summarize, which simply mean going over material again for a useful purpose. A teacher who reviews a chapter before an exam is being helpful. A writer who rehashes arguments that have been made for decades is being unoriginal.

In writing or journalism:
"The article rehashed ideas that economists have been debating for 30 years. There was nothing fresh in it."

In film or entertainment:
"The sequel just rehashed the original movie's plot with a different cast. It felt completely uninspired."

In politics or speeches:
"The senator's speech rehashed the same campaign promises from four years ago. The audience had heard it all before."

In academic work:
"The professor told her that her essay rehashed existing research instead of contributing something original."

In everyday conversation:
"We've talked about this so many times. I don't want to rehash the whole argument again tonight."

Rehash is not the same as repetition.

To repeat something means to present it again in basically the same way — no disguise, no reworking.

To rehash something means to rework or repackage it, but so superficially that the substance hasn't changed at all. There's a thin layer of "newness" on the outside, but underneath, it's the exact same thing.

This is why rehashing can actually feel worse than plain repetition. Repetition is at least honest. Rehashing sometimes involves — knowingly or not — presenting old ideas as if they were fresh ones.

Rehash is not the same as revision.

To revise something means to rework it with the genuine goal of improving it — adding new thinking, correcting errors, developing the ideas further. Revision adds real value.

Rehashing changes the packaging. Revision improves the product. They are opposites in spirit.

In casual conversation, rehash is sometimes used more gently, simply meaning "go over something again" — without strong criticism attached.

For example: "Do we really need to rehash all of this right now?" Here, the speaker isn't saying the original discussion was bad or unoriginal. They simply don't want to repeat the same conversation again.

So in spoken, informal contexts, rehash can be mildly neutral. But in writing — journalism, criticism, academic work — it almost always signals disapproval.

To rehash something is to take old ideas or content, repackage them with only superficial changes, and present them again — without adding anything of real value — often making it look newer or more original than it actually is.
13144:
To reify something means to take an abstract idea, concept, or relationship — something that doesn't physically exist as a "thing" — and treat it as if it were a concrete, real, solid, independent object in the world.

The simplest way to put it: reifying = turning a thought into a "thing."
A Simple Analogy to Lock It In

Imagine you and your friends have a running joke. It's not a physical object. It's just a pattern of behaviour and shared memory between people. It lives in interactions.

Now imagine someone says, "The joke has a life of its own now" or "The joke is taking over our friend group." They're treating "the joke" as if it has agency, weight, and independent existence — as if it were an entity that can act on its own.

That's reification. You took something that only exists as a social, mental, or relational phenomenon and mentally solidified it into a thing.

The world is full of abstractions — things that exist only as ideas, patterns, processes, or relationships, not as physical objects you can touch. Examples:

  • Justice
  • The economy
  • Love
  • Society
  • Race
  • Time
  • Democracy

None of these is a brick you can hold. They're complex, shifting, human-made constructs or processes.

When you reify them, you start speaking about — and more importantly, thinking about — them as though they are fixed, independent, concrete things with their own properties, their own existence, sometimes even their own will.

Example 1 — "The market decided."
Markets aren't single decision-makers. A market is millions of individual human choices, behaviours, social norms, power structures, and historical forces all interacting. But when someone says "the market decided," they collapse all that complexity into a single, concrete-seeming entity that has made a decision. The market has been reified.

Example 2 — "Society is to blame."
Society isn't a person or an object. It's a web of relationships, institutions, and shared norms among people. But when we say "society is to blame," we treat it like a unified agent that has done something. Society has been reified.

Example 3 — "Time is running out."
Time is a concept, a measurement, a dimension of experience. It doesn't literally run. But we speak of it as if it were a substance being depleted from a container. Time has been reified.

Example 4 — "Race determines outcomes."
Race is a social and historical construct — a category humans invented and assigned meaning to. It has no biological solidity. But when people treat racial categories as fixed, natural, self-evidently real properties that people simply have, they are reifying race. The social construction has been turned into a "thing."
The Critical/Philosophical Dimension (Where the Word Is Most Powerful)

Reification becomes a genuinely important concept when it causes harm or hides truth. Here's why:

When you reify something that is actually a human-made construct or a social arrangement, you can make it seem:

  • Natural — as though it has always existed and must exist
  • Inevitable — as though it cannot be changed
  • Objective — as though it exists outside of human choices and history

This is dangerous because it strips away agency. If "the economy" is a real, solid thing operating on its own laws, then humans can't change it — they can only react to it. But if you de-reify that thought and remember that the economy is a set of human-created rules, institutions, and choices, then suddenly it becomes something that can be redesigned.

This is why thinkers in philosophy, sociology, and critical theory use "reify" as a concept for exposing a mental trap: we forget that we built the cage, and so we stop thinking we can leave it.

To reify a social construct is to forget its history — and forgetting its history makes it feel eternal.

Not all uses of "reify" carry this critical weight. In computer science, to reify something means to make an abstract concept into an explicit, first-class object within a system so that it can be manipulated and used directly.

For example, in programming, a "query" is a conceptual request for data. If a language reifies queries — turns them into actual objects in the code — then programmers can store them, pass them around, and operate on them like any other object. Here, reification is simply useful and practical. There's no criticism implied.

So in technical contexts, to reify = to make something abstract into something you can directly work with.
How to Recognise Reification in the Wild

Ask yourself: Is this person treating an idea or a process as though it were a fixed, concrete, self-existing thing?

Signals to watch for:

  • An abstraction is given agency ("the institution decided," "nature wants," "capitalism demands")
  • A process is spoken about as a static object (instead of "people discriminating," someone says "discrimination is just how things are")
  • A constructed category is treated as a natural kind — something that exists in the world independently of human thought and history
  • Something changeable is spoken of as inevitable

When you spot these, you're likely watching reification in action.

To reify is to take something abstract — an idea, a relationship, a social construct, a process — and treat it as though it is a concrete, fixed, independent thing that simply exists in the world.

The word is used critically (to expose a way of thinking that hides human agency and historical contingency) and technically (to make an abstract concept usable and manipulable in a system). Either way, the core action is the same: turning an abstraction into a "thing."
13145:
A reign is the period of time during which a king, queen, emperor, empress, or any supreme ruler holds power. It is the entire stretch of their time in authority — from the moment they take the throne to the moment they leave it, whether through death, removal from power, or voluntary stepping down.

Think of it as an era defined by who is in charge at the very top.
Simple examples in the primary sense

"Queen Victoria's reign lasted 63 years."
→ Victoria was the ruling queen of Britain for 63 years.

"The reign of Emperor Augustus brought stability to Rome."
→ During the time Augustus was emperor, Rome was relatively stable.

"His reign ended when he was overthrown."
→ His time as supreme ruler came to a close when people removed him from power.

A reign isn't just a count of years on a throne. It encompasses everything that happened during that period — the wars, the achievements, the failures, the laws made, the culture of the time. This is why historians place events "during the reign of" a particular ruler: they are giving you the context of who held ultimate authority when those events occurred.

So when someone says "this happened during the reign of King Henry VIII," they mean both when it happened and under whose supreme authority it happened. The two ideas are bundled together in one word.
The figurative meaning (beyond kings and queens)

Reign is not limited to royalty. It is widely used to describe any period in which a person, a force, an idea, or an entity is completely dominant in its domain.

"During his reign as CEO, the company became the world's largest."
→ The period during which he was the top authority, and the company thrived under him.

"Scientists say the dinosaurs' reign on Earth lasted over 160 million years."
→ The long era during which dinosaurs were the dominant creatures on the planet.

"After decades of dominance, the champion's reign finally came to an end."
→ The period during which that champion was supreme in their sport.

In these figurative uses, reign communicates something stronger than just "time" or "era." It implies supremacy — the subject isn't merely present during that period, it dominates it completely.
The emotional weight and connotation of the word

This is a subtle but important point. Reign carries a sense of grandeur and significance. It suggests authority that is absolute, or close to it. This is precisely why writers and speakers choose it over neutral alternatives like "time," "period," or "era" — those words are flat and descriptive. Reign tells you that whoever or whatever is being described stood at the very top, unchallenged, during that stretch of time.

This also means the word can be used ironically or negatively to describe something undesirable that dominated a period: "the reign of chaos," "the reign of mediocrity." Here, the word isn't praising what reigned — it's dramatizing just how thoroughly that thing dominated.

Reign of terror — A period defined by extreme violence, fear, and brutality inflicted upon people. It is most famously used to describe a violent phase of the French Revolution (1793–94), but it is applied broadly whenever a situation is thoroughly defined by fear and suffering.

Reign supreme — To be the most powerful, dominant, or successful in a particular area. "In the 1990s, grunge music reigned supreme." (Note: this uses the verb form of reign, but the meaning is the same — to occupy the position of supreme dominance.)

A long reign / a short reign — Plain descriptions of the duration of someone's time at the top.
Don't confuse reign with these two words

Because "reign," "rein," and "rain" are all pronounced identically, mixing them up in writing is one of the most common mistakes in English. Here is the clear distinction:

Rein is the strap or cord used to guide and control a horse. Figuratively, "to rein something in" means to restrain or limit it ("the government tried to rein in spending"), and "free rein" means the freedom to act as one chooses ("she was given free rein to redesign the office").

Rain is water falling from the sky as precipitation.

Reign alone carries the meaning of ruling, supreme authority, and the period of that authority.

A useful memory trick: reign contains the word king hiding inside it if you look — it has a "g" that hints at royalty, and is the only one of the three that has anything to do with power.

Reign, as a noun, is the period during which someone or something holds supreme power or dominance. It always has a beginning and an end. It applies literally to monarchs and rulers, and figuratively to any person, force, creature, or idea that stands at the top of its domain for a stretch of time. The word carries weight — it signals that the authority in question was not ordinary or partial, but supreme and defining of its era.
13146:
When someone reigns, they hold the highest position of power over a place or people — and that position is officially recognized and unchallenged. Think of a king or queen sitting on a throne. They don't just work there. They are the supreme authority. That is what it means to reign.

The verb "to reign" means to hold supreme power or authority, especially as a monarch.
The Literal Meaning (Its Most Common Use)

In its most direct sense, "reign" is used for kings, queens, emperors, empresses — any ruler of royal status.

  • Queen Victoria reigned over the British Empire for 63 years.
  • The emperor reigned during a time of great peace.

Notice the feeling behind these sentences. It's not just about doing a job. It carries a sense of grandeur, of being the one and only supreme figure at the top.
A Crucial Nuance: "Reign" Is Not the Same as "Rule"

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word.

To reign means to hold the position of a monarch — to officially be the king or queen.

To rule means to actively exercise power — to make decisions, give orders, and govern.

A monarch can reign without ruling. This is exactly what happens in modern constitutional monarchies like the United Kingdom. The King of England reigns — he is officially the monarch, the head of state — but he does not rule in practice. The elected government actually runs the country and makes the laws.

So you might say:

  • The king reigns, but the prime minister rules.

This is not a contradiction. It means: the king holds the royal position, but real governing power belongs to the prime minister.

Think of it this way: reigning is about status and position; ruling is about action and power.
The Figurative Meaning (Used Far Beyond Kings and Queens)

"Reign" is very commonly used outside of royal contexts. When something is completely dominant, unchallenged, or prevails over everything else in a situation, we say it reigns.

  • After the earthquake, chaos reigned in the city. — Chaos was completely in control. Nothing could stop it or compete with it.
  • Silence reigned in the courtroom. — The silence was total and undisturbed, as if silence itself were the king of the room.
  • For two decades, she reigned as the greatest tennis player in the world. — She was supreme, unmatched, at the very top.

The figurative meaning always carries the same essential feeling as the literal one: something is at the very top, with no serious challenger.
"Reign Supreme" — A Common and Important Phrase

You will often see the verb used in the phrase "reign supreme." This simply intensifies the meaning. When something reigns supreme, it is not merely dominant — it is the undisputed, absolute top.

  • In the 1990s, grunge music reigned supreme.
  • In this jungle, the lion reigns supreme.

The word "supreme" reinforces that there is nothing above it, nothing equal to it.

When you want to name what is being reigned over, you use the preposition "over."

  • She reigned over a vast empire.
  • Fear reigned over the entire population.
  • He reigned over the fashion industry for thirty years.

Every time you use or read the word "reign," it carries a certain weight and dignity. It suggests:

  • A long or significant period of dominance, not just a brief moment.
  • An official, recognized, or undeniable status — not just someone who thinks they're in charge.
  • A sense of grandeur or importance.

If you said "he ruled the tennis world," it sounds powerful but ordinary. If you said "he reigned over the tennis world," it sounds historic, majestic, and absolute.
To reign means to hold a position of supreme, unchallenged authority — whether as an actual monarch over a kingdom, or figuratively as the most dominant force in any situation.
13147:
To reimburse someone means to pay them back money they already spent — usually because they spent it on your behalf, or because of something you caused.

The most important thing to understand is the sequence of events:

  1. Someone spends their own money first.
  2. Then you pay them back that same amount.

Without that sequence — money spent first, money returned later — the word doesn't apply.
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine your colleague buys printer ink for the office using his own wallet. It costs $30. Since he bought it for work, the company pays him back that $30.

"The company reimbursed him for the printer ink."

He is out of pocket → the company pays him back → he is reimbursed. That's it.

The structure of the verb is almost always:

[Person/Organisation] reimburses [Person] for [Expense]

Here are the most natural real-world situations:

1. Employer → Employee
This is the most common context. Employees often spend their own money on work-related things — travel, meals, supplies — and then submit receipts so the company can pay them back.

"My employer reimbursed me for the flight tickets."
"She was reimbursed for her hotel stay during the business trip."

2. Insurance Company → Policyholder
You pay a medical or repair bill out of your own pocket first, then the insurance company pays you back.

"The insurance company reimbursed him for the hospital bill."

3. Government → Citizen
Governments sometimes refund people for certain approved expenses, like healthcare or education costs.

"The government reimbursed families for tutoring expenses."

4. One Person → Another Person
In everyday life, if a friend pays for something on your behalf, you reimburse them later.

"She paid for my train ticket, and I reimbursed her the next day."

You can only use "reimburse" when real money was actually spent first. The reimbursement is specifically the return of that spent amount.

If no money was spent yet, you wouldn't use this word. For example, you wouldn't say "I will reimburse you before you buy it." That makes no sense with this word — the spending must come first.

The verb "reimburse" is used in a few very consistent patterns. Learn these and you'll use the word correctly every time.

  • Reimburse someone for something:

"The company reimbursed her for the taxi fare."

  • Reimburse someone's expenses:

"We will reimburse your travel expenses."

  • Be reimbursed (passive voice — very common):

"All volunteers will be reimbursed for their costs."
"He was never reimbursed for the damage."

  • Reimburse someone in full:

"She was reimbursed in full after submitting the receipts."
("In full" means the entire amount was paid back, not just part of it.)
How It Differs From Similar Words

Reimburse vs. Refund
A refund is when a store or seller gives your money back — usually because you returned a product or a service was cancelled. The relationship is between a buyer and a seller.
"The shop refunded me because the jacket was torn."

A reimbursement is between two people/parties where one paid on behalf of the other — not a buyer-seller return situation.
"My employer reimbursed me for buying the jacket I needed for the work event."

Reimburse vs. Compensate
Compensate is broader. It covers paying someone for loss, damage, suffering, or inconvenience — not just for money they spent. You can compensate someone for their time, their pain, or their lost opportunity.
"The airline compensated passengers for the 10-hour delay." (This could be vouchers, upgrades, or money — not necessarily a specific amount they spent.)

Reimburse is more precise — it's specifically about paying back an exact amount someone spent.

Reimburse vs. Pay back / Repay
Pay back and repay usually refer to returning borrowed money (a loan, a debt). The money was lent, not spent on someone's behalf.
"I borrowed $50 from her and paid her back on Friday."

Reimburse implies the money was spent for a purpose (usually for you or your organisation), not just borrowed.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Reimburse" is a formal word. You'll see it a lot in professional, business, legal, and financial contexts — expense forms, insurance policies, employment contracts, and official letters.

In casual everyday conversation, people tend to say "pay you back" instead:

  • Formal: "You will be reimbursed within 10 business days."
  • Casual: "I'll pay you back tomorrow."

Both mean the same thing, but "reimburse" carries a professional, official tone.

If you ever want to check whether "reimburse" is the right word, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Did someone already spend their own money? ✅
  2. Are they being paid back that amount? ✅

If both answers are yes — that's reimbursement.
13148: A rein is a long, narrow strap — usually made of leather — that a rider holds in their hands to control a horse. That's the literal, physical object. But this word carries a much bigger life than just horse equipment, and understanding both sides of it fully is what will make it truly stick.

Picture a horse with a rider on its back. Inside the horse's mouth sits a small metal bar called a bit. The reins are straps connected to that bit, running back to the rider's hands.

The rider steers and commands the horse entirely through the reins:

  • Pull the left rein → the horse turns left.
  • Pull the right rein → the horse turns right.
  • Pull both reins back → the horse slows down or stops.
  • Loosen the reins → the horse moves more freely.

So a rein is fundamentally a tool of control — the physical link between the rider's intention and the horse's movement. Without the reins, the rider has almost no reliable way to guide the horse.

Reins almost always come in pairs (one on each side), which is why you'll most commonly see the plural form: reins.
The Figurative Meaning — And This Is Where It Gets Rich

Because reins are tools of control and guidance, the word has been extended far beyond horses. In everyday language, "reins" is used to talk about control, authority, and power over anything — a country, a company, a situation, a person's impulses.

When someone says "the reins" in a non-horse context, they mean the position of control or the power to direct something. Think of it like this: just as a rider holds the reins to guide a horse, a leader holds the reins to guide an organization.

Here are the most important figurative uses you'll encounter:

1. "The reins of power / government / leadership"

This means the position of control over something — a country, a company, a team, etc.

"After the election, the new president took the reins of government."

The image is: the country is like a powerful horse, and whoever holds the reins is the one steering it.

2. "To hold the reins"

This means to be in charge or to currently have control over something.

"She has held the reins of this company for fifteen years."

3. "To take the reins" (also: "to hand over the reins")

  • Take the reins = to assume control or leadership.
  • Hand over the reins = to give up control and pass it to someone else.

"When the CEO retired, his daughter took the reins."
"He handed over the reins to his successor after thirty years."

4. "Free rein"

This is one of the most commonly used — and most commonly misspelled — phrases in the English language, so pay close attention.

Free rein means the freedom to act however you wish, without restriction.

"The director gave the designer free rein to create whatever she wanted."

The image comes from a rider loosening or dropping the reins entirely, giving the horse full freedom to run as it pleases. When you give someone "free rein," you are essentially dropping the straps — letting them go without control or limits.

⚠️ Common mistake: Many people write this as "free reign" (as in the reign of a king). That is incorrect. The correct phrase is free rein — because the image is of horse reins, not royal power. This is one of the most frequent spelling errors in English, so knowing this puts you ahead of most people.

5. "Give someone the reins" / "pass the reins"

These mean to transfer control or responsibility to another person.

"The founder finally passed the reins to the next generation."
A Key Distinction: Rein vs. Reign

Since these two words sound identical when spoken, they get confused constantly. Here is the difference:

  • Rein → horse strap → control, guidance (what this article is about)
  • Reign → a monarch's rule → a king or queen reigns over a kingdom

The only connection between them is that both involve the idea of power and control — but they are completely different words with different spellings and different roots. When you see rein, always think horse strap first.

A rein is a strap of control. Literally, it controls a horse. Figuratively, it represents any kind of authority, leadership, or power over something. The strength of this word is in that image: something powerful (a horse, a nation, a business) being guided by whoever holds the straps.

When you hold the reins → you are in control.
When you give free rein → you release control.
When you take the reins → you step into control.

That single, elegant image of a rider's hands holding leather straps is behind every use of this word, in every context you'll ever find it.
13149:
To rein something means to control, limit, or pull back something that is moving too freely, growing too fast, or getting out of hand.

The image behind this word is simple and powerful: think of a horse with reins — the long leather straps a rider holds to guide the animal. When the horse moves too fast or in the wrong direction, the rider pulls on the reins to slow it down or bring it back in line. The verb "rein" captures exactly that action — but applied to anything in life, not just horses.

In modern English, "rein" as a verb almost always appears as the phrasal verb "rein in." This is the form you will encounter in real life. Here's what it means precisely:

To rein in = to bring something under control; to deliberately slow down, limit, or restrain something before it goes too far.

Notice two things packed inside this meaning:

  1. Something is already moving — growing, escalating, or running loose.
  2. You are pulling it back — actively, with effort, before it gets worse.

This is subtly different from simply stopping something. Stopping is abrupt and complete. Reining in is more like gradually tightening your grip to bring something back to a reasonable, manageable level — just like a rider doesn't yank a horse to a dead halt but steadily pulls to slow it down.

Notice how the word works across many different situations — the object changes, but the meaning stays the same:

Spending / Finance:

"The company needs to rein in its costs before it goes bankrupt."

The costs are growing out of control. Someone must pull them back.

Emotions:

"He tried to rein in his anger, but it was hard."

His anger was rising fast. He was trying to suppress and control it.

Power / Authority:

"Parliament voted to rein in the President's powers."

The President's powers were seen as going too far. Parliament wanted to limit them.

A person's behavior:

"The teacher had to rein in the rowdy students."

The students were becoming unruly. The teacher brought them back under control.

A broader situation:

"The central bank raised interest rates to rein in inflation."

Inflation was rising too fast. The bank took action to slow it down.

In every single example, you can picture someone pulling on reins — something is running ahead, and a conscious effort is being made to bring it back.

"Rein in" is not a neutral word. It carries a quiet implication that things have already gone too far, or are in danger of doing so. When someone says they need to rein something in, there is an underlying sense of urgency or concern — a warning that without this control, the situation will become a problem.

This makes it stronger and more specific than simply saying "control" or "manage." You use "rein in" when something feels like it is getting out of hand and needs to be actively pulled back.

To fully understand a word, it helps to know its opposite. The opposite of reining something in is the expression "give free rein to" something — meaning to allow it complete freedom, with no restrictions at all.

"The director gave the actor free rein to interpret the role however he wanted."

So: reining in = pulling back and limiting. Free rein = releasing all control and letting something flow freely. These two expressions sit at opposite ends of the same spectrum.

This word is very frequently misspelled, even by native speakers. People often write "reign in" (wrong) or "rain in" (wrong) because all three words sound identical.

  • Rain is the water that falls from the sky.
  • Reign means to rule as a king or queen.
  • Rein is the strap used to control a horse — and the verb we are discussing.

The correct spelling is always rein in. A helpful trick: remember that reins control horses, and the verb comes from that image. If you can picture the leather strap, you'll spell it right.

"Rein in" means to actively bring something under control — to slow it down, limit it, or pull it back before it exceeds what is acceptable or manageable. It always involves something that was moving or growing freely, and a deliberate effort to restrain it. It is stronger than "control" because it implies urgency and the sense that something was already getting out of hand.
